newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: TENNIS-THAI, TAIWANESE PLAYERS EMERGE ASIAN HEROINES.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-THAI, TAIWANESE PLAYERS EMERGE ASIAN HEROINES.

text.p: A pair of unlikely players from Taiwan and Thailand head a long queue of Asian women at the Australian Open hoping to succeed Kimiko Date as the region's new pin-up girl.
Wang Shi-Ting, a shy 23-year-old, and Bangkok teenager Tamarine Tanasugarn have overshadowed their Japanese counterparts to advance to the third round at Melbourne Park.
Nine Japanese players were among the 128 women starters in the year's first grand slam event, but by the end of the second round only tiny Rika Hiraki remained.
A Korean and Indonesian completed the list of 13 Asian women in the draw.
Date, who reached a career-high world ranking of four, was the darling of the Japanese media before her retirement last year and a role model for her Asian contemporaries.
Before the emergence of Date and Chinese-American Michael Chang last decade, Asians thought they simply did not have the physique to challenge the bigger Western players.
"After Kimiko reached the top 10 in the rankings, a lot of others thought, 'if she can do it, why can't we'?" said Wang, who ousted Jolene Watanabe on Thursday 7-5 6-3.
"She was not big and did not have a big serve."
Wang, who stands at 1.71 metres (five ft seven inches), is the tallest of the Asian women still alive in the tournament. Tanasugarn is 1.65 metres tall while Hiraki is only 1.57 metres.
Coached by her father Wen-Chih, the right-hander has never advanced beyond the third round of a grand slam and next meets a tough opponent in ninth seed Karina Habsudova of Slovakia.

Wang, world ranked 40, was looking forward to a second round match on a show court against former teen prodigy Jennifer Capriati, but the American's shock first round loss to Watanabe pushed the Taiwanese player out on to Court 18.
Tanasugarn's third-round berth is the best grand slam performance by a Thai player.

Her dream run, which has captured newspaper headlines in Bangkok, looks destined to come to an abrupt halt in the next round. The 19-year-old, ranked 66 in the world, faces seventh seeded American Lindsay Davenport.
Hiraki, ranked 86, was the lone Japanese survivor at the end of the second round afer she staged a sensational comeback against 10th seed Brenda Schultz-McCarthy of the Netherlands on Wednesday.
Trailing Schultz-McCarthy 0-6, Hiraki fought back to take the next two sets to seal a third round berth against American Kimberly Po.
Po eliminated Asia's top ranked player, world number 29 Ai Sugiyama, of Japan, in a tight three-set dual.
